Jamie — looping in concise guidance and a simple pros/cons matrix (below). Attached: network_matrix_v1.xlsx (matrix + checklist) and a short connectivity checklist PDF.

Summary recommendation (short): for Arbiter Health’s constraints (PHI-adjacent, latency target ~30ms, sustained 400–800 QPS), our preference is to pilot with PrivateLink (interface endpoints) and then, if you need slightly lower deterministic latency and you control the peer VPC, migrate to VPC peering for production. Reasons: PrivateLink gives isolated, customer-controlled endpoints that avoid broad route table exposure; it also simplifies auditing because traffic terminates at an RW-managed endpoint. Peering offers marginally lower hop-count latency but increases routing surface area and requires you to coordinate CIDR management carefully. A site-to-site VPN is acceptable for an initial pilot but is brittle at high sustained QPS and may complicate failover planning (BGP convergence variability).

Short pros/cons:
- PrivateLink (interface endpoints) — Pros: strong isolation (no route table injection), easy IP allowlisting, works with strict egress policies, simplifies audit/tracing per-tenant; Cons: additional ENI consumption on the vendor side, potential slightly higher p50 latency vs peering (~5–10ms observed at similar regions), per-endpoint cost.
- VPC Peering — Pros: lowest added latency, native routing once established, no per-endpoint charges; Cons: route table management required, cross-account peering limits may apply, harder to carve out per-tenant egress controls (you must implement security groups/NACLs).
- Site-to-site VPN — Pros: fast to stand up, works if you cannot allow peering or interface endpoints in your environment; Cons: higher jitter, throughput limits on many managed VPNs, BGP failover timing can introduce transient errors during AZ failures.

Operational responsibilities (high level):
- Arbiter: provide VPC CIDRs, maintain device/firewall rules for allowed IPs, own on-prem NAT/firewall config, and support any BGP session if you choose VPN.
- Redwood: provision the PrivateLink endpoints or peering connections, host-side routing and interface management, provide endpoint IPs, list of health-check endpoints and port requirements, and run the inference fleet behind the endpoint. We also provide a connectivity test harness (tcp latency + synthetic QPS) during pilot.

Gotchas we see often:
1) Overlapping CIDRs — peering requires disjoint VPC CIDRs; if you have overlapping networks, PrivateLink is the less risky path.
2) Large burst patterns — VPN appliances can throttle; validate capacity.
3) Firewall stateful timeouts — UDP/long-lived TCP and keepalives matter for persistent inference sessions (LLM streaming).
4) Service discovery expectations — with PrivateLink you must route to the endpoint DNS names we provide, not to arbitrary IPs.

Next step suggestion:
- Step 1 (pilot): enable a PrivateLink endpoint in your staging account, run 72–96 hour synthetic QPS + latency test with Redwood’s harness.
- Step 2 (optimize): if the staging metrics meet your p50/p95 targets and you prefer simpler routing, schedule a maintenance window to evaluate cross-account VPC peering for production (requires CIDR readiness).

I attached network_matrix_v1.xlsx which includes an estimated cost delta for each pattern at your projected QPS range and a short runbook.

Happy to run a 30m call this week to walk through the matrix — propose Fri 20 Nov 10:00am PT.
